title: Girl, You'll Be a Woman Soon

meta.title: Who originally recorded "Girl, You'll Be a Woman Soon"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Urge Overkill. Neil Diamond wrote it and recorded it first — a Bang Records single from March 1967 that reached No. 10 in the US.
meta.ogTitle: Who originally recorded 'Girl, You'll Be a Woman Soon'?
meta.ogDescription: Urge Overkill's Pulp Fiction version is a cover. Neil Diamond wrote and first recorded the song, released on Bang Records in March 1967.

answer.label: Not an Urge Overkill original — a 1967 Neil Diamond single on Bang Records
answer.sourceLine: Because Uma Thurman dances to it in Pulp Fiction, a great many people file “Girl, You’ll Be a Woman Soon” under Urge Overkill. The song was written by Neil Diamond and first recorded by him, released as a Bang Records single in March 1967 with “You’ll Forget” on the B-side. Diamond’s record was no obscurity either — it reached No. 10 on the US pop singles chart and led off his album Just for You. Urge Overkill’s version came much later, cut for their 1992 EP Stull.

original.heading: Who recorded it first
original.label: Bang Records
original.released: Issued as a 7-inch single on Bang Records in March 1967, backed with “You’ll Forget” in the US and UK and with “New Orleans” in continental Europe. It also opened side A of Diamond’s 1967 Bang album Just for You (BLPS-217).
original.charted: A genuine hit, not a lost original: No. 10 on the US pop singles chart in 1967. It later reached No. 27 on the Dutch Mega Top 100 in 1971.
original.cover: Urge Overkill’s version led off their EP Stull (Touch and Go Records, 10 October 1992), produced by Kramer. After Pulp Fiction used it in 1994, MCA released it as a single: No. 59 on the Billboard Hot 100, No. 11 on Modern Rock Tracks, No. 37 in the UK, No. 10 in France and Flanders, No. 19 in New Zealand and No. 1 in Iceland.

trail: Wikipedia’s article on the song states plainly that it was written by Neil Diamond, whose recording of it on Bang Records reached number 10 on the US pop singles chart in 1967 — see the article ↗.
MusicBrainz places the original recording as track A1 of the 1967 Bang album Just for You (catalogue BLPS-217), timed at 2:48 — the release entry ↗.
Urge Overkill’s version is documented as the opening track of Stull, released by Touch and Go Records on 10 October 1992 — before Pulp Fiction — the EP article ↗.
Wikidata records the song as an original written, composed and performed by Neil Diamond, published 1967 — entity Q1797642 ↗.

authors.name: Neil Diamond
authors.kicker: The original recording artist — and the writer
authors.heading: Neil Diamond
authors.bio: Diamond came up writing for other acts in the Brill Building orbit before Bang Records turned him into a performer in his own right. “Girl, You’ll Be a Woman Soon” belongs to the extraordinary Bang run that also produced “Solitary Man,” “Cherry, Cherry” and “Red, Red Wine” — all of them, like this one, gathered onto Just for You in 1967. Jeff Barry and Ellie Greenwich produced the session; Diamond wrote the words and music alone.

authors.name: Urge Overkill
authors.heading: Urge Overkill
authors.bio: The Chicago trio recorded the song for Stull, a six-track EP issued by Touch and Go Records on 10 October 1992 and produced by Kramer. Quentin Tarantino picked it for Pulp Fiction two years on, and MCA pushed it as a single; it reached No. 59 on the Billboard Hot 100, No. 11 on Modern Rock Tracks, No. 37 in the UK and No. 1 in Iceland. Theirs is a genuinely fine reading — slower, heavier, sung slightly off the beat — and the only thing wrong with the popular account of it is the chronology.

misattribution.heading: The record, corrected
misattribution.intro: The confusion here is purely chronological — Urge Overkill made a memorable record of a song that already existed, and the film that carried it did not stop to say so.

items.why: Their version, first released on the EP Stull in October 1992 and later attached to Pulp Fiction, is the one most listeners know. It is a cover.
Recorded in 1966 and issued as a Bang Records single in March 1967, backed with “You’ll Forget.” It reached No. 10 on the US pop singles chart.
Diamond wrote both words and music. Jeff Barry and Ellie Greenwich produced the original session; they did not write the song.

misattribution.truthLine: Written and first recorded by Neil Diamond, released March 1967 on Bang Records. Urge Overkill’s celebrated version dates from 1992.

context.heading: How a Top 10 hit got mistaken for a cover’s original
lead: The odd thing about this one is that the original was not obscure. Diamond’s single went Top 10 in America. But it arrived in a crowded run of Bang singles, it was never his signature record, and by the 1990s it had settled into the deep shelf of a catalogue better known for “Sweet Caroline.” Urge Overkill’s version had no such competition — it was the only thing most listeners had ever heard the song called.

What sealed it was the placement rather than the record. In Pulp Fiction the song is not background: it plays over one of the film’s most-quoted scenes, and the soundtrack album sold in the millions. A generation met the song there, in a specific arrangement, sung by a specific band, with no sleeve note pointing backwards. That is usually enough.
detailsBody: 1966 — Neil Diamond records the song for Bang Records, produced by Jeff Barry and Ellie Greenwich.
March 1967 — Bang issues it as a single, backed with “You’ll Forget” in the US and UK (“New Orleans” in continental Europe).
1967 — It reaches No. 10 on the US pop singles chart and opens side A of Diamond’s album Just for You.
1968 — Cliff Richard cuts a version, released as the B-side of “I’ll Love You Forever Today”; Jackie Edwards also records it.
10 October 1992 — Urge Overkill’s version leads off the EP Stull on Touch and Go Records, produced by Kramer.
1994 — Quentin Tarantino uses the Urge Overkill recording in Pulp Fiction; MCA releases it as a single late that year and it charts across Europe and Australasia.
context.pull: The original was a Top 10 hit. It still lost the credit.
